still_true: Wegovy's branded US list price is still $1,349 a month and still printed on the box. Almost nobody pays it, and now almost nobody even uses it as a reference point.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed in January 2026 is still off the Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels, and the 503B compounding exclusion finalised from the April 2026 proposal still stands.

The September 2027 Labor/HHS/Treasury wellness guidance is unchanged. It still allows up to a 30% premium differential tied to fill-verified GLP-1 adherence or BMI outcomes, with a reasonable-alternative standard.
Illinois's ban on adherence-conditioned premiums is still the only one of its kind in force. California's bill is still pending in committee.
Tirzepatide has no US generic and is still sold only by Lilly. Lilly still leads on efficacy, now with retatrutide as well.

population.note: FICTIONAL. Arithmetic: 29.5% ever-used minus 23.0% current = 6.5% of adults who used and are off now. 45% of ever-users have cycled, which is 13.3 points: ~11.0 points are current users on at least their second course (48% of current users) and ~2.3 points are cyclers who are off again. The other ~4.2 points stopped once and never restarted. This fits one-year persistence of roughly one-third and restart rates of 36–47%, and cheap generics have pushed restarts toward the top of that range. Of ~267M adults, 23% is ~61.4M current users and 29.5% is ~78.8M ever-users. FICTIONAL payer mix: Medicare ~15M (24%; ~13.5M are 65+, ~19% of ~71M seniors), Medicaid ~10.5M (17%), so public programmes pay for ~41.5% of users and are the largest payer. Commercial ~15M (24%), legitimate cash ~19M (31%, mostly generic semaglutide at $45–75), gray market ~1.9M (3%, mostly tirzepatide and retatrutide 'research peptide' vials). Sum: 15 + 10.5 + 15 + 19 + 1.9 = 61.4M. Age-band check against a 20/33/24/23 adult age mix: 2.8 + 7.6 + 8.2 + 4.4 ≈ 23.0. The income gap narrowed (bottom third 11% → 20%) because $45 generics and 31 Medicaid opt-in states reached people who had been priced out. The remaining floor is income, not price: the ~26M uninsured, people on Medicaid in the 19 non-covering states, and people for whom $45 plus a visit fee is still a utility bill. Adult obesity is ~32.5%, and ~17% of adults have obesity and have never used a drug. Under-18 use (1.4%) rose mostly through Medicaid, where EPSDT obliges states to cover medically necessary drugs for 12–17-year-olds even where adult coverage is optional.

access.public_coverage: Public programmes became the default payer under existing law, with no new statute. Medicare: once generic semaglutide reached ~$55/month gross, Part D plans dropped most prior authorisation for the cardiovascular, CKD, sleep-apnoea, MASH and diabetes codes. Tirzepatide's dementia-risk label still requires PA. Medicare users went from ~8M to ~15M. FICTIONAL Medicare arithmetic: ~11M on generic semaglutide × $55 × 12 ≈ $7.3B, plus ~4M on branded tirzepatide, retatrutide or Wegovy pill × ~$320 net × 12 ≈ $15.4B, for ≈ $22.6B annualised Part D spend in 2030. Bimagrumab infusions are billed separately under Part B and are not included. Medicaid: generic net cost after rebates is ~$38/month, and 31 states plus DC now cover weight management (up from 9 still covering in 2028). ~10.5M users × $38 × 12 ≈ $4.8B combined federal-state, mostly generic.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Indian generic semaglutide costs $5–35/month and has 80+ brands. Indian makers (Dr. Reddy's among the US settlement licensees) now also ship FDA-approved product to the US. Generics are available in ~175 countries. China supplies most of the world's peptide API. Tirzepatide generics have begun launching in India and Brazil where its patents are weaker.
access.note: FICTIONAL. The January 2030 licensed-generic entry for injectable semaglutide (Viatris, Sandoz, Dr. Reddy's, plus Novo's own authorised generic) put pens at $45–75/month cash at Cost Plus, Costco and the chains. The TrumpRx-era channel has been rebranded and folded into manufacturer direct sites under the administration that took office in January 2029. Branded oral Wegovy stays branded (separate formulation patents) at $99 starting and $199 maintenance cash. Lilly cut Zepbound vials to $249–399 cash to hold share, and Foundayo is $129–249. Employer coverage climbed back to 51% (Business Group on Health, 2030) but is mostly generic-first step therapy, and ~3.6M employees are in fill-verified metabolic tracks. Route mix: generic injectables are ~45% of users and orals ~38%, the rest branded injectables. The needle came back for lower-income users because the cheap product is a pen. The gray market fell from ~3M to ~1.9M users and moved to tirzepatide and pre-approval retatrutide knockoffs.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic and, since Jan 2030, licensed generics)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved Mar 2029)
GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist, weekly injectable (survodutide, approved Oct 2029, obesity with MASH)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg; Rybelsus; low-dose oral semaglutide for alcohol use disorder, May 2030)
Activin type II receptor antibody, 4-weekly IV infusion, adjunct to incretin therapy for lean-mass preservation (bimagrumab, Lilly, approved Mar 2030)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda and generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: reduction of risk of all-cause dementia in adults with obesity and established cardiovascular disease (tirzepatide; confirmatory trial ongoing)
alcohol use disorder (low-dose oral semaglutide, May 2030)
preservation of lean mass during incretin-induced weight loss (bimagrumab adjunct, adults 18+, label based on DXA lean-mass endpoint; fracture outcome trial required)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'quiet mind' / focus / food-noise subscriptions on low-dose generic semaglutide sold through telehealth, the most common off-label use
dementia-prevention use without cardiovascular disease, 55–70-year-olds, cash-paid on generic semaglutide
nicotine, gambling and compulsive-shopping reduction (observational support only)
bimagrumab for 'body recomposition' by lean non-obese cash payers at infusion lounges
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
drugs.pipeline_note: The mood_and_motivation driver cannot be met with an FDA mood indication, because there are no adequate trials. It is realised through what the approval rules allow. The phase 3 oral semaglutide alcohol-use-disorder programme was filed (sNDA, May 2029) and approved in May 2030 at a low dose. Novo's 'Turn down the noise' campaign and telehealth 'quiet mind' subscriptions extend it into mood and focus marketing, which drew an FDA OPDP untitled letter in Aug 2030. The muscle-preserving-combo driver is realised by bimagrumab: Lilly's BLA was filed Jan 2029 off the phase 3 programme and approved Mar 2030 (14 months) as an adjunct to tirzepatide or semaglutide. In the pivotal trial, lean-mass loss was cut by roughly two-thirds on DXA, with no fracture endpoint. It is a 4-weekly IV infusion (list ~$1,800/month), with ~350k US users by end 2030, mostly Medicare Part B women 65+. The subcutaneous form is in phase 2 and not on the market. Retatrutide was approved Mar 2029 after the extended review, with a dysesthesia warning (label ~26% weight loss at the top dose). Survodutide was approved Oct 2029. Amycretin was filed Apr 2029 and its review was extended to a Q1 2031 action date. MariTide was filed Feb 2030 and its decision falls in 2031, so it is not on the market. Generic semaglutide arrived through the Jun 2029 Paragraph IV settlement, with ANDAs approved Nov 2029. No generic tirzepatide or oral semaglutide exists in the US. Novo's US semaglutide revenue fell sharply in 2030, while global incretin volume keeps rising.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. Retatrutide's top dose has the highest GI discontinuation rate in the class.

safety_ledger.effect: Gastroparesis / persistent gastric dysmotility, ileus, and pulmonary aspiration under anaesthesia
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Delayed gastric emptying is mechanistic and expected. Whether it persists after stopping is still disputed: a 2029 claims study found a gastroparesis diagnosis HR ~1.6 versus SGLT2 users, with absolute risk under 1% and heavy diagnostic overlap. Registered claims in MDL 3094 (E.D. Pa.) passed ~95,000 by late 2030. The first bellwether (Nov 2029) returned a $38M verdict against Novo, and a Lilly bellwether was a defence verdict. Under Mensing preemption, generic makers cannot be sued for failure to warn, so plaintiffs target brand makers for injuries on generic product too.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Ileus labelled since 2023. ASA pre-procedure holding guidance updated in 2029. No new FDA warning. Settlement framework talks have not concluded.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Elevated with rapid weight loss, and higher with retatrutide.

Outcome trials still show no causal confirmation and absolute risk is low. Pancreatitis and a pancreatic-cancer theory backed by plaintiff experts have joined the gastroparesis claims in the mass tort. Epidemiology does not support the cancer claim.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled. The older MDL settlements were absorbed into the larger tort.

safety_ledger.effect: Lean mass (muscle) loss and bone-density loss
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: The class warning stands. The 2028 hip-fracture HR of ~1.3 in long-term users 65+ was replicated in a 2030 Danish registry. Bimagrumab is marketed as the answer, but it is proven only on DXA lean mass, and its effect on bone density and fractures is unknown. Most older users on $55 generic semaglutide do not get it.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Jul 2028 class labelling and the CMS DXA code continue. A bimagrumab fracture-outcome postmarketing requirement was set (readout ~2034).

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts are still conflicting; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Listed as an adverse reaction; no class warning.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new signal, including in the AUD trials.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: The 2027 cohort figure (~7% vs ~3%) was roughly replicated in 2029. The AUD trial's own exploratory anhedonia scale showed a small dose-related shift. The effect partly reverses after 3–5 weeks off weekly semaglutide but within days on Foundayo (shorter half-life), which shapes how people take drug holidays.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: The FDA postmarketing observational study is ongoing. The AUD label mentions 'decreased interest or enjoyment' in adverse reactions. OPDP untitled letter on 'quiet mind' promotion (Aug 2030).

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Half to two-thirds regain within 18 months. Cheap generics turned cycling from forced (lost coverage) into chosen (holidays, events).
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly. Obesity Medicine Association holiday guidance (2029) advises against repeated full stops in patients 65+.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Case series continue, concentrated in low-dose 'quiet mind' users who eat very little.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: In professional guidance; no label change.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years; adolescents on decades-long therapy; repeated cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About eight years of follow-up exists. Adolescent use is rising through Medicaid EPSDT. There are still no peak-bone-mass data. The first pediatric postmarketing bone report is due 2032.

FICTIONAL: Reports tied to unapproved semaglutide fell after generic entry. Harms have shifted to tirzepatide and retatrutide 'research peptide' vials, and to mg/unit errors among people switching from vials to generic pens.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Import alerts and CBP seizures continue. Personal-importation enforcement is still weak but matters less.

safety_ledger.effect: Retatrutide dysesthesia (skin sensitivity, tingling) and heart-rate increase
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Dysesthesia in roughly 1 in 10 at top dose, mostly mild and dose-related.

safety_ledger.effect: Bimagrumab adjunct effects (muscle spasms, diarrhoea, acne; theoretical cardiac and reproductive effects of activin blockade)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Muscle spasms are common early. The long-term cardiac and reproductive effects of activin-pathway blockade are unknown. The label excludes pregnancy.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled at approval with contraception counselling; cardiac safety postmarketing study required.

food_and_beverage.state: About 40% of US households now have a user. Snack and confectionery volumes are down ~8–10% from 2025 and sugary drinks ~8%. The new pressure point is the bottom third: Dollar General and regional dollar chains in the rural South report soda and snack volume declines after Medicaid opt-ins and $45 pens. Price and pack engineering still hold dollar sales near flat. A small, loud premium segment sells the opposite of 'GLP-1 friendly': full-fat dairy, butcher-counter meat, sourdough, and 'unmedicated' branding aimed at the new appetite aesthetic.

alcohol.state: US spirits volumes are down ~11% from 2025 and beer ~7%. The May 2030 AUD approval made off-label drinking reduction respectable and reimbursable. Distillers keep consolidating capacity, and non-alcoholic lines now make up mid-single-digit shares of portfolios. On-premise late hours keep shrinking in mid-sized cities.

restaurants.state: National traffic is roughly flat to down 1%, and the average check is still under pressure. Casual chains run permanent small-plate menus. A counter-trend is concentrated on the Los Angeles Westside, in Miami and in Brooklyn: steakhouses, churrascarias and 'tasting-length' dinners are booked by people for whom visibly eating a lot is the point. Buffets keep closing.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep shrinking, though more slowly. Mainstream retailers sell to a cycling market with stretch fabrics and rental. Upper-income demand has moved to tailoring for shoulders and thighs ('built, not small'), and athletic brands push heavier-fit lines.

fitness.state: Strength remains the growth market. DXA chains are expanding, and some now partner with bimagrumab infusion lounges. Boutique gyms in Austin and LA advertise 'unmedicated' classes and accept consumer lab certificates ($129 semaglutide/tirzepatide-negative panels) for a members' leaderboard.

insurance.state: Generic substitution cut employer GLP-1 spending per user by roughly half, and pharmacy trend slowed to ~+4–5% in 2030. Employer coverage recovered to 51%, mostly generic-first. Fill-verified metabolic tracks (~3.6M employees) persist under the 2027 guidance and now fight with drug holidays. Medicare is the largest payer, and its actuaries flag Part D incretin spend (~$22.6B annualised) plus open-ended bimagrumab Part B billing.

pharma.state: Novo's US semaglutide revenue fell sharply after January 2030, offset partly by the oral franchise and the AUD label. Lilly grows on tirzepatide, retatrutide and bimagrumab and keeps the premium tier. Indian makers are now legal US suppliers. Both brand makers carry mass-tort reserves and are negotiating a settlement framework.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: A lean, soft body now reads as cheap: a $45 pen, a Medicaid card, a call-centre job. Muscle with visible appetite reads as money and time. 'Unmedicated' is the scarcest claim and the most doubted one. 'Natty or not', borrowed from bodybuilding, is ordinary gossip.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The tiers have flipped. Thinness is mass-market. Upper-income women 25–40 in coastal cities have moved to a 'fed' look of muscle, some softness and big public meals, achieved by lifting, by bimagrumab, or by quietly staying on a low dose. Lower-income users are thin on generics and read as medicated. Older adults on Medicare generics are thin and, in the case of the uninfused, frail.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals in most households are still short and small. In affluent circles the large dinner has returned as display: ordering dessert is a social statement. The church fasting networks continue. Holidays are now organised around drug holidays: weekly-semaglutide users skip three weeks before Thanksgiving, and Foundayo users skip from Wednesday.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: The 'on/off' app markers have been joined by 'natty' badges, which carry no verification. Desire mismatch is still a top couples-therapy complaint, now with named fixes: synchronised holidays, switching one partner to the short half-life pill.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite has moved from noise to status. It still means noise in clinics and employer tracks. In fashion, food media and the gym it means vitality, and the Unmuted collective's language ('being hungry is being here') has been taken up by brands they despise.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Measured clinically meaningful blunting is still ~7% vs ~3% in controls. A 2030 national survey found ~38% of current users had taken a planned dose reduction or holiday in the past year, most often citing 'flatness', sex, or a celebration, and only secondarily GI symptoms.
interior_life.framing: Mostly a side effect that people manage with dose-downs and holidays. Employers call the same thing 'steadiness', and Novo's AUD campaign and the telehealth subscriptions sell it as 'quiet mind'. The words differ by who is paying, and most people use all three.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Fill-verified tracks still penalise gaps. After the 2029 OMA guidance, large vendors accept 'clinician-documented holidays' of up to 4 weeks a year. Smaller plans do not, and the EEOC ADA charges are still unresolved. Some knowledge workers take 'quiet mind' microdoses for focus during crunch periods, then drop them for launches and pitches where they want edge.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: 'Flat' fiction has peaked and is now parodied. The Unmuted 'off nights' have grown into 'Off Week' festivals in Philadelphia and Brooklyn, timed so that weekly users can actually be off. Sportsbook handle keeps lagging among identifiable users. Loud, sour and spicy is still a genre.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Drug holidays are planned around anniversaries, weddings and attempts to conceive (the labels advise stopping semaglutide two months before). Couples schedule desire. Therapists report the reverse complaint too: partners who prefer their spouse on the drug.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: The coalition against adherence premiums lost momentum once cheap generics made coverage less decisive, and California's bill is stalled. Politics shifted to the courtroom, through the mass tort, and to advertising, with a bipartisan Senate letter on 'quiet mind' marketing that produced no legislation. There is still no measurable effect on turnout.

state.regulatory_posture: Routine and fast on approvals (retatrutide, survodutide, bimagrumab, the AUD indication). Generic peptide ANDAs were approved on the liraglutide precedent. OPDP enforcement is limited to untitled letters. The administration that took office in January 2029 launched no new incretin programme. Import alerts continue.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No new subsidy, mandate or statute. Public coverage widened through existing Part D indication rules and state Medicaid optional-drug choices once generic prices fell. Wellness-differential guidance from 2027 unchanged.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Unchanged in law. PBM fill data and app logs still feed wellness vendors. The five state employee plans with monitored tracks and the two Medicaid programmes tying continued coverage to 6- and 12-month adherence and BMI progress still operate.
state.workforce_or_military: The Army oral pilot continues and TRICARE rules are unchanged. DOT still has not ruled on drivers' off-label alcohol-reduction use, which the AUD label now partly converts to on-label use.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: Indian firms went from mail-order adversaries to licensed suppliers. China's peptide API dominance is the new supply-chain talking point. The US–India price gap has narrowed from ~30× to ~3–5× for semaglutide but remains ~20× for tirzepatide.

events.event: Novo Nordisk settles Paragraph IV litigation with Viatris, Sandoz and Dr. Reddy's, licensing US entry of generic injectable semaglutide from January 2030. Novo will launch its own authorised generic. Analysts call it a trade of two years of exclusivity for ending its secondary-patent risk.

The first bellwether trial in GLP-1 MDL 3094 ends in a $38M verdict against Novo for persistent gastroparesis. Registered claims pass 90,000, and because generic makers are shielded by preemption, plaintiffs' firms recruit generic users to sue brand makers.

FDA approves Lilly's bimagrumab as a 4-weekly infusion adjunct to incretin therapy on a DXA lean-mass endpoint, with a fracture-outcome trial required after approval. Lilly's launch tagline is 'Strong, not small.'

FDA approves low-dose oral semaglutide for alcohol use disorder. Within weeks, Novo's 'Turn down the noise' ads and telehealth 'quiet mind' subscriptions on $45 generic pens draw an FDA untitled letter over implied mood claims.

IQVIA data show Medicare and Medicaid now pay for ~41% of US incretin users, overtaking commercial insurance. Part D plans have dropped prior authorisation for generic semaglutide on cardiac, kidney and sleep-apnoea codes, and 31 states now cover it in Medicaid.

The Obesity Medicine Association publishes the first clinical guidance on planned dose reductions and 'drug holidays', after a survey finds more than a third of users take them. Major wellness vendors begin accepting documented holidays in adherence tracks.

open_tensions: The mass tort is aimed at the wrong defendants by design. Most users are now on generic semaglutide, whose makers are shielded by preemption, so a settlement framework with Novo and Lilly would price injuries partly caused by competitors' product, and neither brand maker has agreed.

Public programmes are now the default payer without anyone having voted for it. Medicare's ~$22.6B annualised Part D incretin spend and open-ended Part B bimagrumab billing will meet the next CBO baseline, and there is no statute to defend or cut.

The same reward-dampening that employers reward as 'steadiness' and Novo sells as 'quiet mind' is what a third of users take holidays to escape. Fill-verified premium programmes are still legal under the 2027 guidance and still collide with clinically endorsed holidays.

Thinness has become cheap and muscle has become the scarce, purchasable status. The 'skinny-frail' fix is an expensive infusion proven only on DXA, so frail older adults on $55 generics and adolescents entering through Medicaid are the people least likely to get it.

prose.headline: Thin Is Cheap Now: semaglutide costs $45, Medicare is the biggest payer, and the new luxury is being visibly hungry
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2030 nearly one American adult in four is taking an incretin drug, and three in ten have tried one. The number that changed everything is forty-five dollars. In January, generic semaglutide pens arrived under a patent settlement Novo Nordisk signed the previous summer. Within weeks they were on the shelf at Costco and Cost Plus for less than a phone bill. Wegovy's branded box still says $1,349. It has become a museum label.

The cheap pen did not make the drug free. It moved the barrier. Medicare didn't need Congress. Once a month of semaglutide cost Part D plans about fifty-five dollars, they stopped making doctors fight for it under the heart, kidney and sleep-apnoea codes that already allowed it. Medicare users nearly doubled, to about fifteen million. Thirty-one states now cover it in Medicaid, because at thirty-eight dollars a month net it no longer wrecks a budget. Together the two programmes pay for more users than employers do, and Medicare actuaries now carry a twenty-two-billion-dollar annual line nobody voted for. What remains is a floor of income rather than price: the uninsured, the nineteen Medicaid states that still decline, and the people for whom forty-five dollars is still forty-five dollars.

The drugs have multiplied at the top. Lilly's retatrutide, approved last spring with a warning about tingling skin, takes off about a quarter of body weight. Lilly also sells the other half of the answer. Bimagrumab is a monthly infusion that preserves muscle during weight loss. It was approved in March on scans showing far less muscle loss, though no trial has yet shown fewer broken hips. Its tagline is 'Strong, not small.' About three hundred and fifty thousand people take it, most of them older women whose Part B bills are now being studied.

In May, Novo's low-dose pill was approved for alcohol use disorder. Its advertising said 'Turn down the noise', and telehealth companies began selling 'quiet mind' subscriptions built on generic pens to people who want to focus, or to stop wanting things so loudly. The FDA sent a letter objecting to the implied mood claims. The subscriptions continue.

The flattening is no longer a rumour or a perk. It is a complaint, and managing it is part of ordinary use. A third of users took a planned break last year. People on the weekly shot skip three weeks before a wedding. People on Lilly's shorter-lived pill skip from Wednesday. Last autumn obesity doctors published the first guidance on how to do it. Some wellness programmes that tie premiums to proof of adherence now accept a documented holiday, and others do not.

In a Philadelphia federal courtroom, the gastroparesis litigation has become one of the largest mass torts in the country, with more than ninety thousand claims. A jury awarded thirty-eight million dollars in the first trial. Because generic makers cannot be sued for failure to warn, lawyers sign up generic users to sue the brand makers, who object that they did not make the pen.

When everyone can be thin, thinness stops meaning much. On the Los Angeles Westside, in Miami and in Brooklyn, the expensive body is muscled and a little soft, and it orders dessert in public. Gyms in Austin post lab certificates showing members test negative for the drugs. The question 'natty or not' has left the bodybuilding forums. Dollar stores in Mississippi sell less soda. Plus-size chains keep closing. Steakhouses fill. Most people are somewhere in the middle: on it, off it, between doses, feeling better and a little quieter, and arguing about whether that's the same thing.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Tamika Rowe wakes at five-forty in Columbus, Ohio. Her pen sits in the butter compartment of the fridge, with a pharmacy sticker that says SEMAGLUTIDE, no brand, $3.00 Medicaid copay. She doesn't touch it. Her sister's wedding is Saturday, and this is week three off. Yesterday, for the first time since spring, she wanted fried bologna, and she cried a little at the stove, not from sadness.

Her first client is Mr. Halvorsen, eighty-one, thin as a coat hanger. His infusion card for the muscle drug is clipped to the refrigerator, and his daughter booked him into the lounge on Henderson Road. Tamika steadies him to the shower. He says his legs feel like somebody else's. She says that means they're working.

At lunch her phone shows an ad, a woman in linen on a dock: Turn down the noise. Tamika's noise is back, and she finds she likes it. She eats the whole sandwich.

Her daughter Kiara, sixteen, is at the gym after school with her friends. They are lifting, and they are loudly not on anything. Kiara texts a picture of a deadlift and then, separately: did u eat lol.

At seven Tamika tries on the bridesmaid dress. It pulls a little across the stomach. She stands sideways in the mirror for a long time. Then she calls her sister and laughs about the cake: three tiers, real buttercream. Half the guests won't touch it, her sister says, and the other half will make a show of eating it.

Tamika says she'll be the first kind on Sunday. Saturday she'll be the second.
